analysis.investment_thesis: DCB Bank is a dirt-cheap regional lender with a stunning PEG of ~0.30 (P/E 8.59 / 28.9% profit CAGR) and P/B at 1.0x, making it a classic Lynch "fast grower priced as a slow grower." However, NIM compression risk (finance costs growing at 26.5% CAGR vs. revenue at 16.3%) and a dangerously low promoter stake of 16.23% cap the conviction level.
key_strengths: PEG ratio of ~0.30 — net profit CAGR of 28.9% with P/E of only 8.59; deeply undervalued on earnings growth
P/B at 1.0x provides book-value floor; forward P/E of 6.54 implies market pricing in zero future growth
Asset book compounding at ~19.8% CAGR (₹44,793 Cr → ₹76,810 Cr in 3 years), showing strong loan-book expansion
key_risks: Finance costs growing 26.5% CAGR vs revenue at 16.3% — NIM squeeze is the core structural threat to this story
ROE of only 10.81% — below my 12% threshold; a bank that can't earn adequately on equity is a mediocre franchise
Promoter stake of just 16.23% is a serious governance red flag — skin in the game is dangerously low for a lending institution
red_flags: Operating CF negative 2 of 4 years (₹-441 Cr in 2025) — even adjusting for loan book growth, this volatility is unsettling
Finance cost CAGR (26.5%) materially outpacing revenue CAGR (16.3%) signals cost of funds rising faster than yields
analysis.detailed_analysis:
On pure Lynch math, DCB Bank looks like a screaming bargain: a PEG of 0.30 would make me sit up in my chair. Net profits went from ₹288 Cr to ₹615 Cr in three years — a near-doubling — while the stock trades at just 8.59x trailing earnings and exactly 1.0x book. That's the kind of mismatch between price and reality I built Magellan on. DII holding of 32.8% tells me the smart Indian institutional money has noticed, and the asset base growth to ₹76,810 Cr shows real business momentum, not accounting tricks.

But here's where I pump the brakes: this is a small regional bank competing against HDFC, Kotak, and 12 public sector giants, and the NIM story is deteriorating. Finance costs are compounding at 26.5% while revenue grows at only 16.3% — that gap will eat into profits unless lending yields catch up fast. ROE at 10.81% is uninspiring for a bank; great lenders earn 15-18% on equity. And 16.23% promoter holding is a red flag I can't ignore — when insiders don't own much of the business, I get nervous. I'd watch the next two quarterly NIM prints before buying aggressively.
